images.caption: Hambleton Peninsula, Rutland Water. looking SW from the eastern end of this spit of land that juts out into the middle of the reservoir. This shows the southern arm of the "lake". Note how low the water is, normal level is up to the taller grasses to the left.

images.caption: Hambleton Wood, Rutland Water. On the south shore of the Hambleton peninsula, this wood is managed by the Leicestershire and Rutland Wildlife Trust. In the photo you can see the rabbit fencing protecting the newly coppiced hazel. This is nightingale breeding site.

images.caption:
Grazing above Rutland Water reservoir.
The sheep seem unconcerned by visitors walking along the footpath above their pasture, but they are separated by a fence.  In the background is one of the liminological towers in the lake, used to measure water quality and temperature.
images.alt:
Grazing above Rutland Water reservoir.
The sheep seem unconcerned by visitors walking along the footpath above their pasture, but they are separated by a fence.  In the background is one of the liminological towers in the lake, used to measure water quality and temperature.

images.caption: The mediaeval Buttercross in the Market Place of Oakham, Rutland, England. It is a Grade I Listed Building. The buildings behind belong to Oakham School. To the left is School House, built in 1858 on the site of late 16th-century almshouses built by the school's founder, Archdeacon Robert Johnson. To the right is Chapel Close, the school's administrative centre.
images.alt: The mediaeval Buttercross in the Market Place of Oakham, Rutland, England. It is a Grade I Listed Building. The buildings behind belong to Oakham School. To the left is School House, built in 1858 on the site of late 16th-century almshouses built by the school's founder, Archdeacon Robert Johnson. To the right is Chapel Close, the school's administrative centre.

images.caption: The first mill as it is today. In 1785 the mill was extended to its present length with a culvert beneath for the Bonsall Brook. The sough was separated from the brook and brought from the village along the south side of Mill Lane which it crossed by way of the aqueduct to a new overshot wheel.
